A single molecule of sugar can generate over thirty energy units to power every single thing your body does!
That is right, and today we are going to prove how your cells extract every drop of that cellular fuel!
Here is our fifteen second roadmap for today: first, glycolysis and the link reaction; second, the Krebs cycle; third, oxidative phosphorylation; and fourth, fermentation and regulation.
Lace up your walking shoes! Let us jump straight into set number one!
Set number one: three things to remember about glycolysis!
Three things to remember about glycolysis! What is item number one?
Item one: Glycolysis is the first stage of cellular respiration that takes place in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into two pyruvate molecules without using oxygen.
So, Glycolysis is the first stage of cellular respiration that takes place in the cytoplasm and breaks glucose into two pyruvate molecules without using oxygen!
Think of glycolysis like taking a local commuter bus to the station before the main express train even arrives!
A local bus ride in the cytoplasm before oxygen gets involved! What is item number two?
Item two: Glycolysis uses two ATP at the start and makes four ATP, giving a net gain of two ATP.
It uses two ATP at the start and makes four ATP, giving a net gain of two ATP!
Item three: Glycolysis also produces two molecules of NADH, which carry high energy electrons to a later stage.
Two molecules of NADH are produced to carry electrons down the line!
Listen up, because this is a likely exam question: examiners love to ask where glycolysis happens and its net ATP yield.
That is a classic exam question! Now it is time for our first quick recall check.
Where in the cell does glycolysis take place, and what is its net gain of ATP?
Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and yields a net gain of two ATP!
Now for set number two: three things to remember about the link reaction!
Three things to remember about the link reaction! Give us item number one!
Item one: The link reaction happens when oxygen is present, allowing pyruvate to enter the mitochondrion.
The link reaction happens when oxygen is present, allowing pyruvate to enter the mitochondrion!
Think of oxygen as buying a ticket that lets pyruvate pass through the station turnstile into the mitochondrion.
Oxygen opens the ticket gate so pyruvate can enter the mitochondrion! What is item number two?
Item two: Each pyruvate is converted into acetyl coenzyme A inside the mitochondrion.
Each pyruvate is converted into acetyl coenzyme A inside the mitochondrion!
Item three: This reaction releases carbon dioxide and produces one NADH for each pyruvate.
Carbon dioxide is released and one NADH is made for each pyruvate!
Remember, acetyl coenzyme A is the key molecule that actually enters the Krebs cycle.
Acetyl coenzyme A is the ticket into the Krebs cycle! Flag this for a likely exam question.
What molecule is pyruvate converted into during the link reaction before entering the Krebs cycle?
Pyruvate is converted into acetyl coenzyme A during the link reaction!
Moving on to set number three: three things to remember about the Krebs cycle!
Three things to remember about the Krebs cycle! What is item number one?
Item one: The Krebs cycle is a series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix where acetyl coenzyme A combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
The Krebs cycle is a series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix where acetyl coenzyme A combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate!
Let us lock in that definition: The Krebs cycle is a series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix where acetyl coenzyme A combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
Got it! The Krebs cycle is a series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix where acetyl coenzyme A combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate!
Item two: Over a series of steps, citrate is broken down, releasing two carbon dioxide molecules, three NADH, one FADH two, and one ATP per turn.
Each turn releases two carbon dioxide molecules, three NADH, one FADH two, and one ATP!
Here is a quick mnemonic for the products of one turn: Three Naughty Foxes Ate Two Carrots!
Three Naughty Foxes Ate Two Carrots! Three NADH, one FADH two, one ATP, and two carbon dioxide!
Item three: Because one glucose gives two acetyl groups, the Krebs cycle turns twice per glucose.
The Krebs cycle turns twice for every single glucose molecule!
This is definitely a likely exam question: students always forget to double the yield for one whole glucose molecule.
Always multiply by two for one full glucose! Let us test this right now.
How many times does the Krebs cycle turn for each molecule of glucose?
The Krebs cycle turns twice per glucose because one glucose molecule provides two acetyl groups!
Now we reach set number four: three things to remember about oxidative phosphorylation!
Three things to remember about oxidative phosphorylation! Hit us with item number one!
Item one: Oxidative phosphorylation is the process on the inner mitochondrial membrane where electron transport drives proton pumping to produce ATP.
Oxidative phosphorylation is the process on the inner mitochondrial membrane where electron transport drives proton pumping to produce ATP!
Let us say that core definition again: Oxidative phosphorylation is the process on the inner mitochondrial membrane where electron transport drives proton pumping to produce ATP.
Oxidative phosphorylation is the process on the inner mitochondrial membrane where electron transport drives proton pumping to produce ATP!
Item two: As electrons move along the electron transport chain, protons are pumped into the space between the membranes.
Electrons move along the chain like a high speed baggage conveyor belt, pumping protons across!
Then those protons flow back through ATP synthase, which acts like a revolving turnstile driving the creation of ATP.
Protons flow back through the ATP synthase turnstile to generate maximum ATP!
Item three: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with protons to form water.
Oxygen catches the electrons at the end of the line and combines with protons to form water!
Highlight this likely exam question: what molecule serves as the final electron acceptor?
Time for recall check number four!
What is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation, and what does it form?
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, and it combines with protons to form water!
Now for set number five: three things to remember about overall yield and fermentation!
Three things to remember about overall yield and fermentation! What is item number one?
Item one: In total, one glucose molecule can yield about thirty to thirty-two ATP, with most coming from oxidative phosphorylation.
One glucose molecule yields about thirty to thirty-two ATP total, mostly from oxidative phosphorylation!
Item two: Fermentation is an anaerobic process that regenerates NAD plus so glycolysis can continue without oxygen.
Fermentation is an anaerobic process that regenerates NAD plus so glycolysis can continue without oxygen!
Repeat that key definition: Fermentation is an anaerobic process that regenerates NAD plus so glycolysis can continue without oxygen.
Fermentation is an anaerobic process that regenerates NAD plus so glycolysis can continue without oxygen!
Think of fermentation like a emergency backup battery that keeps the basic dashboard lights on when main power fails.
An emergency backup generator! What is item number three?
Item three: Fermentation yields only two ATP per glucose, producing lactate in animals, and ethanol plus carbon dioxide in yeast.
In animals fermentation yields lactate, while in yeast it yields ethanol and carbon dioxide!
Watch out for a likely exam question comparing the end products of fermentation in animals versus yeast.
Let us check our understanding right now with check number five!
Why do cells undergo fermentation when oxygen is absent, and how much ATP does it yield?
Fermentation regenerates NAD plus so glycolysis can keep running, but it yields only two ATP per glucose!
Finally, set number six: three things to remember about the regulation of respiration!
Three things to remember about regulation! Give us item number one!
Item one: Cellular respiration is regulated by the energy needs of the cell to keep supply matched to demand.
Respiration is regulated by the needs of the cell to keep energy supply matched to demand!
Think of it like a smart cruise control system in a car that adjusts fuel consumption to keep speed steady.
A smart cruise control for energy! What is item number two?
Item two: When ATP is plentiful, high ATP levels slow down the enzyme phosphofructokinase in glycolysis.
When ATP is plentiful, it acts as a brake on the enzyme phosphofructokinase!
Item three: When ATP is low and ADP is high, phosphofructokinase speeds up to produce more energy and prevent wasting glucose.
When ATP is low and ADP is high, phosphofructokinase steps on the gas pedal!
This enzyme control mechanism is a very likely exam question on cellular control.
Time for our sixth and final recall pause!
What happens to the enzyme phosphofructokinase when cellular ATP is low and ADP is high?
When ATP is low and ADP is high, the enzyme phosphofructokinase speeds up!
To recap the most important points: Respiration breaks down glucose through glycolysis, the link reaction, the Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation to generate up to thirty-two ATP.
Without oxygen, fermentation keeps glycolysis going for two ATP, while phosphofructokinase regulates the whole pipeline to prevent wasting glucose.
